name: Void Song

detectability.signature: Torus-shaped gravitational anomaly emitting low-frequency harmonic vibrations detectable on gravimetric and acoustic sensors

proximity: Ship hulls resonate at subsonic frequencies, producing an audible hum through structural vibration
Navigation instruments oscillate between current position and exit-point coordinates
contact: Instantaneous translocation to an undetermined exit point approximately 340 light-years distant
Brief but intense electromagnetic pulse fries unshielded secondary systems
Crew experience a momentary sensation of being stretched across infinite distance
prolonged_exposure: Resonant frequencies induce micro-fractures in crystalline components
Crew report persistent auditory hallucinations resembling choral singing
Navigational databases slowly corrupt with phantom coordinate entries

age: Unknown; estimated stable for at least 12,000 years based on stellar drift patterns

behavior.cycle: Aperture diameter oscillates between 600 and 1100 km on a 47-hour cycle

phenomena: A shimmering ring of blue-shifted starlight marks the aperture, showing stars from the exit region superimposed on local space
Gravitational harmonics produce standing waves in nearby dust clouds, sculpting them into concentric shell patterns
Objects passing through the ring cast shadows in two directions simultaneously for a fraction of a second
The interior of the ring appears to contain a tunnel of compressed starfield stretching to an impossible vanishing point
hazards: Transit during aperture minimum risks partial translocation of larger vessels
Exit point is located in an uncharted region with unknown local hazards
Electromagnetic pulse on transit can disable life support if surge protectors fail
opportunities: Provides a 340 light-year shortcut, potentially saving months of conventional travel
Harmonic frequencies could be studied to understand wormhole stabilization mechanics
Exit region may contain unexplored systems with untapped resources
known_incidents: The exploration corvette Nightjar became the first vessel to successfully transit the Void Song in 2387, emerging 340 light-years away near a previously unknown trinary star system; the return journey took fourteen months by conventional drive
A trade consortium attempted to establish a relay beacon at the exit point in 2412, but the beacon's crystalline emitter array shattered within hours from residual harmonic resonance
description: Void Song manifests as a luminous ring suspended in open space, roughly 850 kilometers in radius at its widest. The aperture shimmers with blue-shifted light from distant stars, as though a window has been cut through the fabric of space itself. At its edges, spacetime curves visibly, bending background starfields into elongated arcs that frame the ring like a cosmic iris.

The anomaly pulses on a regular 47-hour cycle, its aperture expanding and contracting like a breathing throat. Ships within sensor range detect a distinctive harmonic signature — a series of gravitational waves that propagate outward in concentric shells, causing hull plating to vibrate at frequencies just below human hearing. Crews universally describe it as singing, a deep and wordless chorus that seems to emanate from nowhere and everywhere at once.

The origin of Void Song remains one of the sector's enduring mysteries. Its regularity and geometric perfection suggest artificial construction, yet no known civilization possesses the capability to engineer stable wormholes. Some xenoarchaeologists theorize it may be a relic of a long-vanished precursor species, while astrophysicists argue it could be a natural phenomenon stabilized by an improbable but not impossible alignment of cosmic strings.

Currently, Void Song serves as both a scientific curiosity and a temptation. Several expeditions have transited successfully, confirming the exit point's location in an unexplored region rich with uncharted systems. However, the one-way nature of the journey and the remoteness of the destination have discouraged commercial exploitation. A small research station maintains a permanent vigil near the aperture, cataloging its pulsations and listening, always listening, to its song.
